title: Impact of Rent Control Expansion on Urban Rental Prices

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with two-way (unit and period) fixed effects.  
Why: We observe treated and untreated districts before and after the expansion of rent control. DID compares the change in average log rents in the treated group to the contemporaneous change in the control group, netting out common shocks.  
Key assumption: Parallel trends – in the absence of the policy, the average log-rental-price trend in treated districts would have moved in parallel to that of untreated districts. We will probe this with a placebo (pre-period only) check.

## 2. R Code
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of Rent Control Expansion on Log Rental Prices
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Packages
required <- c("fixest", "data.table")
new      <- required[!(required %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new)) install.packages(new, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(fixest)     # fast fixed-effects estimators
library(data.table) # fast data handling

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------
file_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s38_data.csv"
df <- fread(file_path)

# 2. Baseline DID with two-way FE -----------------------------
did_fe <- feols(y ~ treated*post | unit_id + period,
                data = df,
                cluster = ~unit_id)     # cluster at district level

# 3. Simple DID without FE ------------------------------------
did_simple <- feols(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post,
                    data = df,
                    cluster = ~unit_id)

# 4. Placebo test (pre-periods only) --------------------------
df_pre <- df[post == 0]                       # keep observations before policy
# create a pseudo-post: last pre period = 1, others = 0
last_pre_period <- max(df_pre$period)
df_pre[, placebo := fifelse(period == last_pre_period, 1, 0)]

placebo_fe <- feols(y ~ treated*placebo | unit_id + period,
                    data = df_pre,
                    cluster = ~unit_id)

# 5. Print main results ---------------------------------------
cat("=== Baseline DID with Unit & Time FE ===\n")
print(summary(did_fe, se = "cluster"))
cat("\nCoefficient of interest (treatment x post):",
    coef(did_fe)["treated:post"], "\n\n")

cat("=== Simple DID (no FE) ===\n")
print(summary(did_simple, se = "cluster"))
cat("\nCoefficient of interest (treat_x_post):",
    coef(did_simple)["treat_x_post"], "\n\n")

cat("=== Placebo Test (pre-periods only) ===\n")
print(summary(placebo_fe, se = "cluster"))
cat("\nCoefficient on fake interaction (treated x placebo):",
    coef(placebo_fe)["treated:placebo"], "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition and prior literature suggest that stricter rent control dampens rental price growth in regulated units while possibly increasing prices in the unregulated segment. Given our aggregated district-level outcome, the net effect should be negative: treated districts’ average log rents should fall relative to controls.  
Magnitude: a semi-elasticity around –0.05 to –0.10 (≈ 5–10 percent reduction) is plausible for a short-run response. If the coefficient on treated × post equals –0.07, for example, it implies rents are roughly 7 percent lower in treated districts after the expansion, conditional on common shocks and fixed effects.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log rental prices over time between treated and untreated districts.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The expansion of rent control policies led to a decrease in log rental prices in treated districts.
